# Simplex compression can increase maximum mixed-integer depth

The proposed monotonicity is false, already for `n=d=1`. In that case a
centered unit-volume simplex is the interval `[-1/2,1/2]`, so simplex
compression replaces every interval fiber by the centered interval of the
same length. The examples below compare the actual maximum over every
point of the mixed set, not just a chosen fiber centroid.

All measures below are unnormalized one-dimensional Hausdorff measure,
equivalently the sum of interval lengths. A nonvertical line through a
selected point `(k,t)` has equation `x=t+s(z-k)`. Its upper closed cap
has mass

    F_{k,t}(s)=sum_j clip(u_j-t-s(j-k),0,u_j-l_j).    (1)

The intersection of this line with each vertical fiber is at most a
point, so it has zero relevant measure. The opposite closed cap therefore
has mass `M-F_{k,t}(s)`. Expression (1) is continuous and piecewise
affine in `s`; its only finite breakpoints come from the endpoint
equalities at indices `j!=k`. Its extrema occur at breakpoints or in the
two constant tails. Closed vertical caps must additionally be checked.
For arbitrary containing halfspaces, shifting the boundary towards the
selected point can only reduce their mass, so these through-point caps
suffice for lower bounds as well as upper bounds.

## A three-fiber example

Take

    C={(z,x):-1<=z<=1, 0<=x<=2-|z|}.

This is a full-dimensional compact convex pentagon. Its integer fibers
at `z=-1,0,1` are `[0,1],[0,2],[0,1]`, of total mass `M=4`.
On either endpoint fiber a sufficiently tilted halfspace isolates either
one-sided piece of that fiber. The smaller of those pieces has length at
most `1/2`, so the endpoint depths are at most `1/8`.

On the middle fiber at `t in [0,1]`, the containing caps

    {x<=z+t}, {x>=t}

have masses `t+1` and `4-3t`, respectively. Hence the unnormalized depth
is at most

    min(t+1,4-3t)<=7/4,

with equality in this bound only at `t=3/4`. For `t in [1,2]`, the second
cap has mass `2-t<=1`. Thus the global maximum is at most `7/16`.
At `(0,3/4)`, the breakpoints of (1) are

    s=-3/4,-1/4,1/4,3/4,
    F(s)=9/4,7/4,7/4,9/4.

Both constant tails have mass `9/4`. Thus every nonvertical containing
cap has mass at least `7/4`; either vertical through-point cap has mass
three. The original maximum is **exactly `7/16`**.

The compressed set has fibers `[-1/2,1/2],[-1,1],[-1/2,1/2]` and is
centrally symmetric about `(0,0)`. Reflection through this point exchanges
the two open sides of every through-point hyperplane, while preserving
measure, so either closed containing halfspace has at least half the
total mass. The horizontal halfspace through this point has mass exactly
half. No point can have depth above half: a horizontal line through any
point has boundary of zero relevant measure, and one of its two closed
sides has mass at most half. The compressed maximum is therefore exactly
`1/2>7/16`.

## A four-fiber example with no fiber carrying half the mass

The following stronger counterexample removes a possible repair based on
excluding a heavy fiber. Let

    P=conv{(0,0),(3,0),(3,3),(2,10),(0,2)}.

It has lower graph zero and upper graph `2+4z` on `[0,2]` and `24-7z`
on `[2,3]`. This upper graph is concave, so `P` is a full-dimensional
compact convex body. Its four integer fibers are

    [0,2], [0,6], [0,10], [0,3]

at indices `0,1,2,3`. The total mass is `M=21`, and its largest fiber
has mass `10<21/2`.

For the endpoint fibers, tilted containing halfspaces isolate the smaller
one-sided fiber portion, giving unnormalized depth bounds `1` and `3/2`.
For the index-one fiber at `t in [0,6]`, choose sufficiently tilted upper
and lower containing caps that include the entire index-zero fiber and
exclude both fibers to the right. Their masses are `2+(6-t)` and `2+t`.
The smaller is at most five.

For the index-two fiber at `t<=4`, a sufficiently steep containing cap
`x<=t+L(z-2)` includes the whole index-three fiber, excludes the two
fibers to the left, and takes length `t` from its own fiber. Its mass is
`3+t<=7`. For `t>=4`, use the containing halfspace

    x>=t+4-2z.

It misses the two left fibers except possibly measure-zero endpoints and
has total mass

    10-t+(5-t)_+<=7.

This proves that the original global maximum is at most `7/21`.
At `(2,4)`, the finite breakpoints and cap masses in (1) are

    s:     -4, -2, -1,  1,  2,  4,
    F(s):   9,  7,  7,  9, 12, 14.

The constant tails have masses nine and fourteen. Therefore all these
upper cap masses lie in `[7,14]`, as do their complementary lower-cap
masses. The vertical through-point caps have masses eighteen and
thirteen. Thus every containing halfspace has mass at least seven and
the original maximum is **exactly `7/21=1/3`**.

Now compress each interval to its center. At `(2,0)`, write `s=-b<=0` in
(1). The upper-cap mass is

    F(-b)=5+(1-2b)_++(3-b)_++min(3,3/2+b), b>=0.

On the four consecutive ranges this is

    21/2-2b,       0<=b<=1/2;
    19/2,          1/2<=b<=3/2;
    11-b,          3/2<=b<=3;
    8,             b>=3.

It lies in `[8,21/2]`. Reflection in the continuous coordinate gives
`F(b)=21-F(-b)`, so all upper and lower nonvertical caps have mass at
least eight. The vertical containing caps have mass at least thirteen.
Thus `(2,0)` has depth `8/21`.

This is also the compressed global maximum. The same endpoint and
index-one bounds `1,3/2,5` remain valid, since translating interval
fibers does not change those limiting-cap bounds. For index two and
`t>=0`, the cap `x>=t-3(z-2)` is contained in the corresponding cap
through `(2,0)`, of mass eight. It therefore gives an upper bound eight.
For `t<=0` reflect this cap across `x=0`. Hence the compressed maximum
is **exactly `8/21>7/21`**.

Compression produces a convex body in each example: its upper graph is
half the original concave length function, and its lower graph is its
negative. It preserves every fiber volume and the set of integer indices.
The failure therefore cannot be attributed to a loss of convexity or a
change in weights. It specifically refutes monotonicity of the maximum
depth under the proposed compression.

The rational cap evaluations and piecewise formulas are checked in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_simplex_compression.py`; the global inequalities above are exact
algebraic bounds and require no numerical optimization.
